items.title: 110 Folding Hunter Knife with Leather Sheath
items.claim: Buck currently lists the standard 110 Folding Hunter as an identifiable product with model SKU 0110BRS-B, giving the founding case a precise subject to test rather than a brand-level nomination.

items.title: Buck 2020 Dealer Catalog: 110 Folding Hunter
items.claim: The standard 110 Folding Hunter is documented with a 3.75-inch 420HC clip-point blade, 4.875-inch closed length, 7.2-ounce weight, wood handle, brass bolsters, leather sheath, and model 0110BRS-B. These specifications describe a substantial traditional sheath-carry folder, not a lightweight pocket-clip form.

items.title: Our Forever Warranty
items.claim: Buck documents a life-of-knife defect warranty, factory repair evaluation, a $6.95 SPA sharpening/polish/adjust service, and $10 420HC blade replacement for folding knives; the published exceptions exclude 110 and 112 Autos, not the standard 110 tested here. Buck states a 10–12 week repair turnaround and requires factory service for disassembly work.

items.title: The History of Buck Knives: Chapter 10
items.claim: Buck's own history records the development of the Folding Hunter as a locking folding knife authorized in 1963, supporting a long, legible model lineage while remaining manufacturer-origin history rather than independent proof of performance.

items.title: Buck 110 Folding Hunter Review | Tested & Rated
items.claim: OutdoorGearLab's comparative test describes the Buck 110 as solid, strong, heavy, without a modern pocket clip, and two-hand opening; it says lighter and more sophisticated knives are better suited to everyday carry and places the Buck closer to a toolbox or fishing kit.
items.notes: The review links to Amazon and is therefore retained as comparative evidence with a commercial disclosure, not as the independent-source floor.

items.title: The Buck Folding Hunter
items.claim: A long-term owner report describes a 1982 Buck 110 carried and used across decades and difficult field conditions, including rope, webbing, wire, stakes, canvas, and sandbags. The report supports the plausibility of long service life but is one owner account, not population-level proof.
items.notes: Contextual longevity record only; not treated as sufficient by itself for a declaration.

items.title: No.08 Stainless Steel Folding Knife
items.claim: Opinel documents the No.08 Stainless Steel Folding Knife as a 3.28-inch, 12C27 stainless blade, 7.59-inch overall length, 1.6-ounce folding knife with a Virobloc safety ring. The page also states manufacture in Chambéry and a limited lifetime warranty limited to manufacturer defects or workmanship exchanges.

items.title: Care & Maintenance: Everything You Need to Know About Your Opinel Knife
items.claim: Opinel publishes user maintenance for sharpening, wooden handles, and Virobloc adjustment, and directs owners to contact the company for a replacement locking ring. The public service record does not establish a standard blade replacement or factory rebuild program for the No.08.

items.title: 2013 Spyderco Product Guide: Delica4 Lightweight
items.claim: Spyderco's official guide identifies the C11BK Delica4 Lightweight with a 4.25-inch closed length, 2.90-inch VG-10 blade, 2.6-ounce weight, back lock, screw-together construction, and four-position ambidextrous clip. The guide positions it as a lightweight everyday-carry folder.

items.title: Warranty & Repair
items.claim: Spyderco offers lifetime warranty coverage, sharpening, regrinding, re-profiling, reassembly, and other paid service, but explicitly states that it does not replace knife blades under any circumstances and that hard-used products may eventually reach the end of service life and should be retired and replaced.

items.title: Edge Retention Testing of Seven More Steels
items.claim: Independent metallurgy and testing context describes 420-family steel as offering high toughness and corrosion resistance because of its low carbide content, while noting that hardness and edge-retention tradeoffs remain. This supports evaluating Buck's 420HC as a maintainable, forgiving steel rather than treating the material name as a complete verdict.
